chapters.n: Moroni begins an abridgment of the Jaredites, an ancient people destroyed in the “north country” long before the Nephites arrived. Their story is a warning to later nations in the same land.

f.g: The land northward, where the Nephites later found Jaredite ruins.

chapters.n: His source is the twenty-four gold plates found by King Limhi’s people, called the Book of Ether after the last Jaredite prophet.
The first part of Ether’s record covered the Creation, Adam, and history up to the great tower. Moroni assumes the Jews already have these things in their scriptures.
So Moroni skips that early history, though it remains on the plates, and whoever finds them may obtain the full account.
He gives only part of the account, from the tower to the people’s destruction.
Ether wrote the record and descended from Coriantor. Moroni now traces Ether’s family line backward to Jared — about thirty generations.

f.g: He lived his whole life in captivity.

chapters.n: Coriantor was the son of Moron, a king who lost the throne and was taken captive.
Moron was the son of Ethem, a wicked king in a time when prophets warned of destruction.
Ethem was the son of Ahah, who ruled briefly but did great evil.
Ahah was the son of Seth, who lived all his days in captivity.
Seth was the son of Shiblon (spelled Shiblom later in Ether), a king whose brother rebelled and killed the prophets.
Shiblon was the son of Com, who regained the kingdom and heeded the prophets late in life.
Com was the son of Coriantum, one of several generations born into captivity.
Coriantum was the son of Amnigaddah, who also lived in captivity.
Amnigaddah was the son of Aaron — not the brother of Moses, but a Jaredite who lived in captivity.
Aaron descended from Heth, son of Hearthom. “Descendant” here signals that some generations may be skipped.
Hearthom was the son of Lib, a righteous and prosperous king who built a great city near the narrow neck of land.
Lib was the son of Kish.
Kish was the son of Corom, a king who did good.
Corom was the son of Levi, who regained the kingdom after years in captivity.
Levi was the son of Kim, who did not rule righteously and was taken captive.
Kim was the son of Morianton, who ruled justly over the people but not over himself.
Morianton descended from Riplakish, an oppressive king with many wives and heavy taxes.
Riplakish was the son of Shez, who rebuilt a broken people.
Shez was the son of Heth, who revived secret combinations and was destroyed by famine.
Heth was the son of Com, a king of the generation after Coriantum.
Com was the son of Coriantum, a righteous king who built many cities.
Coriantum was the son of Emer, a righteous king who saw the Son of Righteousness.
Emer was the son of Omer, who was overthrown by his son Jared but warned in a dream to flee.
Omer was the son of Shule, a just king who restored his father’s kingdom.
Shule was the son of Kib, who was captured by his own son and later freed.
Kib was the son of Orihah, the first Jaredite king, who was the son of Jared himself. The genealogy reaches its starting point.
Jared, his brother, and their friends came from the great tower when the Lord confused the people’s languages and scattered them across the earth.
The brother of Jared was a large, mighty man highly favored by God. Jared asks him to pray that their language not be confused.

f.g: His name is not given in the text; Joseph Smith is reported to have identified it as Mahonri Moriancumer.

chapters.n: He prays, and the Lord in compassion preserves the language of Jared and his brother.
Jared asks him to pray again for their friends, that their language also be spared. Jared’s concern extends beyond his own family.
The Lord has compassion on their friends and families too, and their language is not confused.
Jared asks his brother to inquire whether the Lord will drive them out and where. Perhaps God will lead them to a land choice above all others — and if so, they should be faithful to receive it.
The brother of Jared prays as Jared suggested. The pattern of humble, persistent prayer runs throughout this story.
The Lord hears him and responds with compassion.
God tells him to gather flocks, seeds of every kind, and all their families and friends. Like Noah, they are to prepare for a great journey.

f.g: An expression meaning “Come now” or “Get moving.”

f.w: both male and female, of every kind

chapters.n: He is to lead them into the valley to the north, where the Lord will meet them and go before them to a land choice above all lands.
There God will make of their descendants a great nation, greater than any on earth — all because they have long cried to him. Persistent prayer is rewarded.

f.w: because this long time ye have cried unto me

chapters.n: The group goes down to the valley of Nimrod, named after the famous hunter, with all their flocks. Nimrod in Genesis is linked to the region of Babel.

f.g: “A mighty hunter before the Lord,” whose kingdom included Babel.

chapters.n: They trap birds and even carry fish in a container. They are preparing to establish life in a new land.
They also bring “deseret,” meaning honeybee, along with swarms of bees and seeds of every kind. Utah pioneers later adopted “Deseret” and the beehive as symbols of industry.
In the valley, the Lord comes and speaks to the brother of Jared from a cloud, so he does not see him.
The Lord leads them into uninhabited wilderness, going before them in a cloud and directing their travel — much like Israel in the Exodus.

f.w: where there never had man been

chapters.n: They travel through the wilderness and build barges to cross many waters, continually guided by the Lord’s hand.
The Lord would not let them stop short in the wilderness beyond the sea; he wanted them to reach the promised land, which he had preserved for a righteous people.
God swore that whoever possesses this promised land must serve him, the only true God, or be swept off when his full wrath comes.
Moroni pauses to apply this: the decree applies to every nation in this land. Destruction comes only when they are “ripened in iniquity” — fully ripe in sin.

f.g: Wickedness grown complete, like ripe fruit ready for harvest.

chapters.n: Because the land is choice above all others, its inhabitants must serve God or be swept off. This is God’s everlasting decree — but only when iniquity is full.
Moroni addresses the latter-day Gentiles directly: learn God’s decrees and repent, so you don’t bring down his wrath as earlier inhabitants did.
This choice land will be free from bondage, captivity, and all other nations, if its people serve the God of the land — Jesus Christ.

f.w: the God of the land, who is Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Returning to the story, the Lord brings them to the great sea. They camp on the shore at a place they call Moriancumer and live there in tents for four years.

f.g: Possibly named after the brother of Jared himself.

chapters.n: After four years the Lord appears again in a cloud and talks with the brother of Jared for three hours, rebuking him for not calling on the Lord’s name. Even great prophets can grow lax in prayer.
He repents and prays for his people. The Lord forgives them but warns that his Spirit will not always strive with man; those who sin until fully ripe will be cut off.

f.w: my Spirit will not always strive with man

chapters.n: The Lord tells them to build barges like the ones they had built before. They are small and light on the water, floating like a bird.

f.w: lightness of a fowl upon the water
f.g: Floating high and easily, like a duck.

chapters.n: The barges are watertight “like a dish” on the bottom, sides, top, and door, with peaked ends, and as long as a tree. They are designed to survive being submerged.

f.g: Sealed so no water could leak in.
Their length was the length of a tree.

chapters.n: The brother of Jared tells the Lord he has built the barges as directed.
He raises two problems: there is no light to steer by, and no fresh air to breathe. He brings real, practical concerns to God.
The Lord solves the air problem: make a hole in the top and bottom, unstop it for air, and stop it if water comes in.
The brother of Jared does as commanded.
He prays again: the vessels are ready, but there’s no light. Will the Lord let them cross the great water in darkness?
This time the Lord asks him, “What will ye that I should do?” Windows would shatter, and fire is not allowed. God invites him to think and propose a solution.

f.w: What will ye that I should do

chapters.n: They will be like a whale in the sea, battered by mountainous waves, but God will bring them up again. He controls the winds, rains, and floods.

f.w: as a whale in the midst of the sea

chapters.n: God will prepare them against the waves, winds, and floods — they cannot cross without his help. So he asks again: what do you want me to prepare for light when you are under the sea?
With eight barges ready, the brother of Jared climbs the very high mount Shelem and melts sixteen small, clear stones out of rock — two for each barge. He carries them to the top and prays.

f.g: Melted (smelted) out of rock — he did the work he could before asking God.
Possibly related to a word for height or wholeness; the text says it was named for its height.

chapters.n: He humbly acknowledges human weakness and God’s holiness. Because of the Fall people are prone to evil, yet God has commanded them to call on him and receive according to their desires.

f.w: because of the fall our natures have become evil continually

chapters.n: He recalls that God has disciplined them yet been merciful during years in the wilderness, and pleads that they not cross the raging sea in darkness. Then he presents his stones.
Confident in God’s power, he asks the Lord to touch the stones with his finger so they will shine in the dark vessels during the voyage.

f.w: touch these stones, O Lord, with thy finger

chapters.n: “Thou canst do this.” God’s great power can look small to human understanding — a simple act for God may seem impossible to us.

f.w: looks small unto the understanding of men

chapters.n: The Lord touches each stone, and the veil is removed from the brother of Jared’s eyes. He sees the Lord’s finger, like a man’s finger of flesh and blood, and falls in fear.

f.w: the veil was taken from off the eyes

f.g: Christ’s spirit body looked like the physical body he would later receive.

chapters.n: The Lord asks him gently, “Arise, why hast thou fallen?”
He explains he feared being struck, for he did not know the Lord had flesh and blood. He is surprised that God has a form like a man.

f.w: I knew not that the Lord had flesh and blood

chapters.n: The Lord says that by faith he saw what Christ will become — taking on flesh and blood. No one ever came to him with such great faith. Then he asks, “Sawest thou more than this?”

f.w: I shall take upon me flesh and blood

chapters.n: He answers no, and asks boldly, “Lord, show thyself unto me.”
The Lord tests his faith: will he believe the words the Lord is about to speak?
He replies that he knows the Lord speaks truth and cannot lie. His faith is already confident before hearing the words.
Christ shows himself. Because of this knowledge, the brother of Jared is redeemed from the Fall and brought back into God’s presence.

Christ declares: he was prepared from the foundation of the world to redeem his people; he is Jesus Christ, the Father and the Son. In him all who believe have eternal life and become his sons and daughters.

f.w: prepared from the foundation of the world
I am the Father and the Son

chapters.n: He has never shown himself this way to man, because no one has believed as this man has. All people were created in his image.

f.w: never have I showed myself unto man
f.g: Likely meaning never in this full way, since others such as Adam and Enoch also saw the Lord.

chapters.n: What he sees is the body of Christ’s spirit; humans were created after that spiritual body, and Christ will appear in the flesh just as he now appears in spirit.

f.g: Spirits have form like physical bodies.

chapters.n: Moroni explains he cannot give the full account, but Jesus showed himself in spirit just as he later appeared to the Nephites.

f.w: as he showed himself unto the Nephites

chapters.n: Jesus ministered to him as he did to the Nephites, so he would know Jesus is God.
Because of his knowledge, he could not be kept from seeing within the veil. When he saw the finger, faith became knowledge — he knew, doubting nothing.

f.w: he had faith no longer, for he knew

chapters.n: With this perfect knowledge of God, he was brought within the veil, saw Jesus, and Jesus ministered to him.
The Lord forbids him to share these things with the world until Christ is glorified in the flesh. He is to treasure them up and show no one.
When he comes to the Lord (at his death), he is to write and seal these things in a language no one can read.
The Lord gives him two stones to seal up with his writings. These are interpreters, which Latter-day Saints associate with the Urim and Thummim used by Joseph Smith.
Since the language he will write in has been confused, God will in his time use these stones to make the writing readable to people.

f.g: Make clear, enlarge so it can be understood.

chapters.n: The Lord then shows him all the people who had ever lived and ever would live, to the ends of the earth.

f.w: all the inhabitants of the earth

chapters.n: God had promised to show him all things if he believed. Because he knew the Lord could, nothing could be withheld. Faith opens the windows of revelation.
The Lord commands him to write these things and seal them; the Lord will reveal them in his own time.
He is also to seal up the two stones and not show them until the Lord does.

The Lord told the brother of Jared to come down and write what he saw, but it was not to be revealed until after Christ’s crucifixion. King Mosiah kept these records hidden until Christ appeared to the Nephites.

f.g: Mosiah II translated the Jaredite plates with interpreters.

chapters.n: After Christ visited the Nephites, he commanded that these things be made known.
But the Nephites later fell into unbelief, and only the Lamanites remain, who reject the gospel. So Moroni is commanded to hide the records in the earth again.
Moroni has written on his plates the very things the brother of Jared saw — the greatest revelations ever given. This is the sealed portion of the gold plates.

f.w: there never were greater things made manifest

chapters.n: The Lord commanded Moroni to write and seal these things and to seal up the interpreters too. This is why part of the gold plates was sealed when Joseph Smith received them.
These sealed revelations will not go to the Gentiles until they repent and become clean before the Lord.
When people exercise faith like the brother of Jared and become sanctified, Christ will reveal what he saw and unfold all his revelations. Greater light depends on greater faith.

f.w: even as the brother of Jared did
the Father of the heavens and of the earth

chapters.n: Christ declares that those who fight against or deny his word will be cursed and shown no greater things.

f.w: unto them will I show no greater things

chapters.n: At his command the heavens open and shut, the earth shakes, and people pass away as by fire. Christ is the Lord of all creation.

f.w: the heavens are opened and are shut

chapters.n: Whoever rejects Christ’s words rejects his disciples. If you doubt that Christ is speaking, judge for yourself — you will know at the last day.
Those who believe will be visited by the Spirit and come to know these things are true and bear witness. The Spirit persuades people to do good.

f.w: it persuadeth men to do good

chapters.n: Whatever persuades to do good comes from Christ, the source of all good. Rejecting his words is rejecting him and the Father who sent him. He is the light, life, and truth of the world.

f.w: whatsoever thing persuadeth men to do good is of me
the light, and the life, and the truth of the world

chapters.n: Christ invites the Gentiles to come to him and receive the “greater things” — knowledge hidden only because of unbelief.
He invites Israel too, promising to reveal the great things the Father prepared for them from the beginning, withheld only because of unbelief.

f.w: from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: When they tear away the “veil of unbelief” that keeps them in wickedness, hard hearts, and blind minds, and pray to the Father in Christ’s name with broken hearts, they will see that God remembers his covenant.

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit

chapters.n: Then the revelations given to John (the book of Revelation) will be opened to all. Seeing these things shows that the time is near.
When you receive this record, know that the Father’s work has begun across the land. The Book of Mormon itself signals the latter-day gathering.

f.w: the work of the Father has commenced

chapters.n: Christ calls the whole earth to repent, believe his gospel, and be baptized. Believers who are baptized will be saved, unbelievers condemned, and signs will follow believers.

f.w: he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved

chapters.n: Blessed is the one faithful to Christ’s name at the last day; he will be lifted up into the kingdom prepared for him from the beginning. Christ seals the message with his own word.
Moroni addresses the future translator — whom Latter-day Saints know to be Joseph Smith — telling him not to try to translate the sealed portion until God allows it.
The translator may be allowed to show the plates to those who help bring forth the work.

f.g: Later fulfilled with the Eight Witnesses, among others.

chapters.n: Three people will be shown the plates by God’s power, so they will know with certainty that the record is true. This was fulfilled in the Three Witnesses — Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris — in 1829.

f.w: unto three shall they be shown

chapters.n: By the mouth of three witnesses these things will be established. Their testimony, the record itself, and the witness of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost will stand against the world at the last day.

f.w: in the mouth of three witnesses

chapters.n: Those who repent and come to the Father in Jesus’ name will be received into God’s kingdom. The goal of the witnesses is salvation, not just proof.
If Moroni lacks authority, judge for yourself — but you will know he had it when you see him at the last day before God.

f.w: ye shall know that I have authority

chapters.n: After his long aside to future readers, Moroni resumes the story of Jared and his brother.
The brother of Jared places the Lord-touched stones in the barges, one at each end, and they give light.
So the Lord made stones shine in darkness so men, women, and children would not cross the sea in the dark. God answered the prayer exactly as asked.
They prepare food for themselves and their animals, board the barges, and set out to sea, entrusting themselves to the Lord.
The Lord sends a furious wind blowing toward the promised land, tossing them on the waves. The same wind that frightens them also carries them home.
Huge waves and terrible storms often bury them deep in the sea.

f.w: buried in the depths of the sea

chapters.n: Because the vessels are watertight like a dish and like Noah’s ark, no water hurts them. When surrounded by water they cry to the Lord, and he brings them back to the surface.
The wind never stops blowing toward the promised land the whole time they are at sea. God’s guidance is constant even when it feels rough.
They sing praises to the Lord; the brother of Jared praises and thanks him all day and into the night. Gratitude fills even a frightening voyage.
No sea monster or whale can damage them, and they have light constantly, above or below the water.
They are driven by the wind for 344 days — nearly a year at sea.
Landing on the promised land, they bow down, humble themselves, and weep with joy for the Lord’s many tender mercies.
They spread across the land and begin farming.
Jared has four sons: Jacom, Gilgah, Mahah, and Orihah. Orihah will become the first king.
The brother of Jared also has sons and daughters.
Jared and his brother’s friends number about 22 people, who also had children before arriving, so the population starts to grow.
They are taught to walk humbly before the Lord and are taught “from on high” — by revelation.
They spread out, multiply, farm, and grow strong.
Growing old, the brother of Jared suggests to Jared that they gather and count the people and ask what they want before the two leaders die.
The people gather. The brother of Jared has 22 sons and daughters; Jared has 12 children, including four sons.
After counting them, the leaders ask what the people would like done before they die.
The people ask for one of their sons to be anointed king.

f.g: Pour oil on the head to set apart a king.

chapters.n: This grieves the leaders. The brother of Jared warns that a king leads to captivity — a warning that will prove true throughout Jaredite history.

f.w: Surely this thing leadeth into captivity

chapters.n: But Jared tells his brother to let them have a king, and invites the people to choose one of their sons.
They choose Pagag, the brother of Jared’s firstborn, but he refuses. His father will not force him, commanding that no one be compelled to be king.
All of Pagag’s brothers also refuse.
All of Jared’s sons refuse except Orihah, who is anointed king.

f.w: Orihah was anointed to be king

chapters.n: Under Orihah the people prosper and become very rich.
Jared and his brother die.

f.g: The brother of Jared’s death closes the founding generation.

chapters.n: Orihah walks humbly, remembers what the Lord did for his father, and teaches his people about God’s great works for their ancestors. Remembering is a key to righteousness.

f.w: remember how great things the Lord had done

chapters.n: Orihah, the first king, judges the land righteously for a very long life. The monarchy begins well.
He has thirty-one children, twenty-three of them sons. Large royal families will later fuel rivalries for the throne.
In old age Orihah has Kib, who becomes king after him. Kib’s son is Corihor.
At 32, Corihor rebels and moves to the land of Nehor. His family grows attractive and influential, and he draws many people after him.

f.g: A Jaredite land; unrelated to the later Nephite apostate Nehor (Alma 1).

chapters.n: Corihor raises an army, marches on Moron where the king lives, and captures his own father — fulfilling the brother of Jared’s warning about captivity.

f.w: the saying of the brother of Jared

chapters.n: Moron, the royal seat, was near the land the Nephites later called Desolation.
Kib lives in captivity under his son until very old, and while captive fathers Shule.
Shule is angry at his brother Corihor. He grows physically strong and also wise in judgment.
Shule goes to the hill Ephraim, smelts ore, and makes steel swords for his followers. He then defeats Corihor at Nehor and restores the kingdom to his father.

f.g: A Jaredite hill with metal ore; not the Ephraim of Israel.

chapters.n: For this, Kib gives Shule the kingdom, and he reigns in his father’s place.
Shule judges righteously and extends his kingdom across the land as the population grows.
Shule also has many sons and daughters.
Corihor repents of his evils, and Shule gives him power in the kingdom — a striking example of forgiveness and reconciliation.
Corihor has many children, including a son named Noah (not the Noah of the flood).
Noah rebels against both King Shule and his own father Corihor, drawing away his brother Cohor, his other brothers, and many people. The cycle of rebellion repeats.
Noah wins a battle and takes the land of their first inheritance, becoming king over that region.

f.w: the land of their first inheritance
f.g: Where the Jaredites first settled after landing.

chapters.n: In another battle Noah captures Shule and carries him to Moron.
As Noah prepares to execute Shule, Shule’s sons sneak into Noah’s house at night, kill him, break open the prison, and restore their father to the throne.
Noah’s son continues his kingdom but never again overpowers Shule, whose people prosper greatly.
The land is now split into two kingdoms: Shule’s and Cohor’s (Noah’s son).
Cohor attacks Shule, but Shule defeats and kills him.
Cohor’s son Nimrod gives his kingdom to Shule and wins his favor; Shule treats him generously. A peaceful surrender ends the divided kingdom.

f.g: Named like the ancient hunter after whom the valley of Nimrod was called.

chapters.n: During Shule’s reign, prophets sent by the Lord warn that the people’s wickedness and idolatry are bringing a curse, and they will be destroyed unless they repent.

f.g: Worship of idols or false gods.

chapters.n: The people mock and insult the prophets, but King Shule punishes those who abuse them.
Shule passes a law protecting the prophets’ freedom to go wherever they wish, and as a result the people repent. A righteous leader can protect the voice of God.
Because they repent of sin and idolatry, the Lord spares them and they prosper again. Shule has more children in old age.
No more wars occur in Shule’s days. He remembers how the Lord brought his ancestors across the sea and judges righteously all his life.

f.w: he remembered the great things that the Lord had done

chapters.n: Shule’s son Omer becomes king. Omer has a son named Jared — not the Jared of the tower — who has his own children.
This Jared rebels against his father, moves to the land of Heth, and uses flattering, cunning words until he has won half the kingdom.

f.g: Win people over with insincere praise.

chapters.n: With half the kingdom, Jared fights his father, takes him captive, and forces him to live in captivity.
Omer spends half his reign in captivity. During it he has children, including Esrom and Coriantumr — an earlier Coriantumr, not the last Jaredite king.
Esrom and Coriantumr, furious at their brother Jared, raise an army and attack him at night.
After destroying Jared’s army, they are about to kill him, but he begs for his life and promises to return the kingdom to their father. They spare him.
Jared is deeply sorrowful at losing the kingdom, for he had set his heart on it and on worldly glory. His ambition sets the stage for darker plans.
Jared’s clever daughter sees his sorrow and devises a plan to win back the kingdom for him.
She is very beautiful. She asks her father whether he has read their ancestors’ records, which tell of people who gained kingdoms through secret plans.
She proposes that her father invite Akish; she will dance for him so he wants to marry her, and Jared will demand the king’s head as the price.

f.w: bring unto me the head of my father
f.g: Compare Salome’s dance and John the Baptist’s death.

chapters.n: Akish is a friend of King Omer. When invited, he watches the daughter dance, is pleased, and asks to marry her.
Jared agrees — if Akish brings him the head of his father, the king.
Akish gathers his relatives at Jared’s house and asks them to swear loyalty to whatever he asks.
They swear by God, heaven, earth, and their own heads that anyone who fails to help or reveals Akish’s secrets will die. Secrecy enforced by death defines these combinations.
Akish administers ancient oaths used by power-seekers, handed down from Cain, a murderer from the beginning.
The devil keeps these oaths alive to keep people in darkness and help power-seekers gain power through murder, plunder, lies, and wickedness.
The daughter put the idea into Jared’s heart; Jared put it into Akish’s; and Akish spread it to family and friends with attractive promises. Evil spreads from heart to heart.
They form a secret combination like those of old — the most abominable wickedness in God’s sight.

f.g: A conspiracy bound by secret oaths.

chapters.n: The Lord does not work through secret combinations and has forbidden bloodshed since the beginning.

f.w: the Lord worketh not in secret combinations

chapters.n: Moroni deliberately does not record the details of their oaths, because such things exist among all peoples, including the Lamanites.

f.w: I, Moroni, do not write the manner of their oaths

chapters.n: These combinations caused the destruction of both the Jaredites and the Nephites. They are a proven civilization-killer.

f.w: the destruction of the people of Nephi

chapters.n: Any nation that supports such combinations for power and gain until they spread throughout will be destroyed. God will avenge the blood of his saints.

f.w: cry unto him from the ground

chapters.n: Moroni addresses the latter-day Gentiles: these things are shown so you can repent and not let murderous combinations rise above you, or God’s sword of justice will fall.

f.w: the sword of the justice of the Eternal God

chapters.n: When you see these things among you, wake up to your awful situation. The blood of the slain cries from the dust for vengeance against the combination and its builders.

f.w: awake to a sense of your awful situation

chapters.n: Whoever builds such a combination seeks to overthrow the freedom of all nations. It comes from the devil — the father of lies who deceived Adam and Eve, inspired the first murder, and hardened hearts to kill prophets.

f.w: overthrow the freedom of all lands

chapters.n: Moroni writes this so evil can be done away, Satan can lose his power over hearts, and people can be persuaded to do good continually and come to the fountain of righteousness to be saved.
Moroni continues: through the secret combination of Akish and his friends, Omer’s kingdom is overthrown.
Still, the Lord is merciful to Omer and to his children who did not seek his death.

God warns Omer in a dream to leave. He travels many days past the hill Shim and the place where the Nephites would later be destroyed, then east to Ablom by the seashore, settling there with all his family except Jared.

f.w: the place where the Nephites were destroyed
f.g: Cumorah, called Ramah by the Jaredites (Ether 15:11).

chapters.n: Jared is anointed king “by the hand of wickedness” and gives his daughter to Akish in marriage.
Akish then plots against his own father-in-law. His sworn accomplices behead Jared on his throne while he is meeting with the people.

f.g: Holding a public hearing with subjects.

chapters.n: The secret society has corrupted the whole people, so Jared is murdered and Akish becomes king. Those who gain power by murder often lose it the same way.
Akish grows jealous of his own son, imprisons him, and starves him to death. Secret combinations destroy even family love.
Nimrah, the dead son’s brother, is angry at his father for this.
Nimrah gathers a small band and flees to live with the exiled Omer.
Akish has other sons who win the people’s hearts, even though the people had sworn to serve Akish in all his evil.
The people want money as much as Akish wants power, so the sons bribe them and draw most of the people away. Greed undermines even a conspiracy.
War between Akish and his sons lasts many years until nearly the entire kingdom is destroyed — only thirty people survive, plus those who fled with Omer.

f.g: A near-total collapse; a preview of the final Jaredite destruction.

chapters.n: Omer is restored to his land of inheritance.
In old age Omer fathers Emer and anoints him king.
Omer sees two years of peace before dying, after a long life full of sorrow. Emer follows in his father’s footsteps.

f.w: fill the steps of his father

chapters.n: The Lord begins lifting the curse from the land. Under Emer’s reign the people become strong and very rich over 62 years.
They have every kind of fruit, grain, silk, fine linen, gold, silver, and precious things — a picture of great prosperity.

f.g: Some fine fabric; the exact material is uncertain.

chapters.n: They have cattle, oxen, cows, sheep, swine, goats, and many other animals used for food.
They also have horses, donkeys, elephants, and animals called cureloms and cumoms, which were especially useful. The meaning of these two Jaredite words is unknown.

f.g: Untranslated Jaredite names for animals; their identity is unknown.

chapters.n: So the Lord blesses this choice land, but repeats his decree: those who possess it must serve him or be destroyed when ripened in iniquity.
Emer judges righteously all his life, has many children, and anoints his son Coriantum as king.
Emer lives four more years in peace and even sees the “Son of Righteousness” — Christ — rejoicing in his day before dying in peace.

f.w: rejoice and glory in his day

chapters.n: Coriantum follows his father’s example, builds many great cities, and does good for his people, though he has no children until very old.

f.w: walk in the steps of his father

chapters.n: His wife dies at 102. In old age he marries a young woman and has children, living to 142.
His son Com reigns 49 years and fathers Heth and other children.
As the people spread across the land, wickedness grows again, and Heth embraces the old secret plans to destroy his father.

f.w: the secret plans again of old

chapters.n: Heth kills his father with his own sword and takes the throne.
Prophets again call for repentance, warning that without it a curse will come — a great famine that will destroy them.

f.w: prepare the way of the Lord

chapters.n: The people reject the prophets, drive them out, and throw some into pits to die — all by King Heth’s order.
A severe drought comes; with no rain, people die rapidly.
Poisonous serpents also appear and kill many. Flocks flee south toward the land the Nephites later called Zarahemla.
Many animals die along the way, but some reach the land southward.
The Lord stops the serpents from pursuing the animals and has them block the passage, so anyone trying to pass would be bitten.
The starving people follow the animals’ trail and eat the carcasses until none are left. Facing death, they finally repent and cry to the Lord.
When they humble themselves enough, the Lord sends rain; the people revive and crops grow again. God’s judgments aim at repentance, and his mercy follows humility.
Heth and his household died in the famine, all except Shez. This survivor begins rebuilding a broken people.

f.w: Heth had perished by the famine

chapters.n: Remembering his ancestors’ destruction and how the Lord brought Jared across the sea, Shez builds a righteous kingdom and walks in God’s ways. Memory again fuels righteousness.

f.w: Shez did remember the destruction of his fathers

chapters.n: His eldest son, also named Shez, rebels, but is killed by a robber because of his great wealth, which restores peace to his father.
Shez builds many cities, the people spread again, and he lives to old age. His son Riplakish succeeds him.
Riplakish does evil: he has many wives and concubines, burdens the people with heavy taxes, and uses them to build grand buildings. He resembles Israel’s King Solomon and Nephite King Noah.
He builds a beautiful throne and many prisons. Anyone who resists or cannot pay taxes is imprisoned and forced to labor; those who refuse to work are executed.
He gets his fine goods — even refined gold and fine workmanship — from prison labor, and afflicts the people with his immorality.
After 42 years the people revolt; Riplakish is killed and his descendants driven out. Oppression eventually provokes rebellion.
Years later Morianton, a descendant of Riplakish, raises an army of outcasts, wins city after city in a long, bitter war, and becomes king of all the land.

f.g: Exiles, those driven out of society.

chapters.n: Once king, he lightens the people’s burdens, wins their favor, and they anoint him king.
He is just to the people but not to himself; because of his immorality he is cut off from the Lord’s presence. Public good does not excuse private sin.

f.w: cut off from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: Under Morianton many cities are built, and the people grow rich in buildings, gold, silver, grain, flocks, and herds.
Morianton lives very long and fathers Kim, who reigns eight years before his father dies. Kim does not rule righteously and loses the Lord’s favor.
Kim’s brother rebels and imprisons him for life. In captivity Kim has children, including Levi in his old age.
Levi lives in captivity 42 years after his father’s death, then wars against the reigning king and takes the kingdom.
As king, Levi does right, the people prosper, and he lives long. He anoints his son Corom king.
Corom does good all his days, has many children, and dies like everyone else. Kish succeeds him.

f.w: even like unto the rest of the earth

chapters.n: Kish dies, and Lib becomes king.
Lib also does good. In his days the poisonous serpents are destroyed, so people go south to hunt in the forest-filled land, and Lib himself becomes a great hunter.
They build a great city by the narrow neck of land, where the sea divides the land.
They keep the land southward as a wilderness hunting preserve, while the land northward fills with people.
They are extremely industrious and trade busily with one another for profit.
They mine and work gold, silver, iron, brass, copper, and other metals, piling up great heaps of earth to get ore, and create fine work.

f.w: cast up mighty heaps of earth

chapters.n: They produce silks, fine-twined linen, and all kinds of cloth for clothing.

f.g: High-quality linen woven from tightly twisted thread.

chapters.n: They make all kinds of farm tools for plowing, sowing, reaping, hoeing, and threshing.

f.g: Thresh — beat grain to separate seed from stalk.

chapters.n: They also make tools for working with their animals.
They make all kinds of weapons and highly skilled, intricate craftsmanship.
No people could be more blessed and prospered by the Lord. They live in a land choice above all others, as God declared.
Lib lives many years and fathers Hearthom, among other children.
After 24 years Hearthom loses the kingdom and spends the rest of his life in captivity.
For several generations — Heth, Aaron, Amnigaddah, Coriantum — the royal line lives entirely in captivity, until Com is born.

f.w: dwelt in captivity all his days

chapters.n: Com draws away half the kingdom, rules it 42 years, and after a long war with King Amgid gains the rest of the kingdom.

f.g: The reigning king in Com’s day; mentioned only here.

chapters.n: In Com’s time robbers appear, adopting the old secret plans and oaths to destroy the kingdom. The secret combinations return again.
Com fights them often but cannot defeat them.
In Com’s days many prophets warn that this great people will be destroyed unless they repent and abandon murder and wickedness.
The people reject the prophets and try to kill them, so the prophets flee to King Com for protection.
They prophesy many things to Com, and he is blessed for the rest of his life. Protecting God’s messengers brings blessings.
Com lives to old age; his son Shiblom becomes king. Shiblom’s brother rebels, and a great war spreads across the land.
Shiblom’s brother has all the prophets who foretold destruction put to death. Silencing the warning does not stop the danger.
Great calamity follows. The prophets had warned of a curse and destruction unlike any before, with bones piled like heaps of earth, unless the people repented.

f.w: their bones should become as heaps of earth

chapters.n: Because of their wicked combinations, they ignore the Lord. Wars, contentions, famines, and plagues bring unprecedented destruction in Shiblom’s day.
The people begin to repent, and to the extent they do, the Lord has mercy on them. God’s mercy responds to even partial repentance.

f.g: To the degree that they did.

chapters.n: Shiblom is killed, and his son Seth is taken captive for life.
Seth’s son Ahah gains the kingdom, commits every kind of evil, causes much bloodshed, and dies young.
Ethem, a descendant of Ahah, becomes king and also does evil.
In Ethem’s days many prophets again warn that the Lord will utterly destroy the people unless they repent.
The people harden their hearts; the prophets mourn and withdraw. When warnings are refused, the messengers may be withdrawn.
Ethem judges wickedly all his days. His son Moron succeeds him and is also wicked.
A rebellion arises from the secret combination built for power and gain. A powerful wicked man takes half the kingdom from Moron and holds it for years.
Moron eventually defeats him and regains the whole kingdom.
Another powerful man arises, a descendant of the brother of Jared.
He overthrows Moron, who lives the rest of his life in captivity and fathers Coriantor.
Coriantor lives his entire life in captivity.
In Coriantor’s days many prophets speak of great things, call for repentance, and warn of utter destruction if the people don’t change.
They also prophesy that God will bring another people to possess the land, as he brought the Jaredites — fulfilled when Lehi’s and Mulek’s groups arrived.

f.w: another people to possess the land

chapters.n: The people reject all the prophets’ words because of their secret society and wickedness.
Coriantor fathers Ether, the prophet who wrote this record, and dies in captivity. The genealogy of Ether 1 now reaches its author.
Ether lives during the reign of Coriantumr, king over all the land — the last Jaredite king.

f.g: The people of Zarahemla later found him, the last survivor.

chapters.n: Ether is a prophet of the Lord who cannot be held back from prophesying because of the Spirit within him.
From morning to sunset he urges the people to believe in God and repent or be destroyed, teaching that by faith all things are fulfilled.

f.w: by faith all things are fulfilled

chapters.n: Those who believe in God can confidently hope for a better world at God’s right hand. This hope, born of faith, is an anchor to the soul, making people steady and full of good works.

f.w: maketh an anchor to the souls of men

chapters.n: Ether prophesies marvelous things, but the people disbelieve because they cannot see them.
Moroni explains: faith is hoping for things not seen. Don’t argue because you can’t see; no witness comes until after your faith is tested.

f.w: faith is things which are hoped for and not seen
ye receive no witness until after the trial of your faith

chapters.n: By faith Christ showed himself to the Nephites after his resurrection — but only after they had faith. Some had faith first; he did not appear to the whole world.
Because of human faith, Christ has shown himself, glorified the Father, and opened a way for others to share the heavenly gift and hope for unseen things.
So readers too can have hope and share that gift, if they will only have faith.
By faith ancient leaders were called to the holy order of God — the priesthood.
By faith the law of Moses was given, but in giving his Son God prepared a “more excellent way,” fulfilled through faith.
Without faith, God can perform no miracles among people. He did not show himself until after they had faith. This is the core principle of the chapter.

f.w: God can do no miracle among them

chapters.n: Examples begin: Alma and Amulek’s faith made the prison collapse.
Nephi and Lehi’s faith changed the Lamanites, who were baptized with fire and the Holy Ghost.
Ammon and his brothers’ faith brought a great miracle among the Lamanites — thousands converted.
All miracle-workers, before and after Christ, worked them by faith.
By faith the Three Nephites received the promise not to taste death — and only after showing faith.
No one has worked miracles until after having faith; they first believed in the Son of God.
Many before Christ had faith so strong that they could not be kept outside the veil; they saw with their eyes what they had first seen with the eye of faith.
The brother of Jared was one of these. His faith was so great that God could not hide his finger from him, because of the promise obtained by faith.

f.w: when God put forth his finger

chapters.n: Having seen the finger, he could no longer be kept outside the veil, so the Lord showed him all things.
By faith Moroni’s ancestors obtained the promise that these records would reach their brethren through the Gentiles, so Jesus Christ commanded Moroni to write.
Moroni confesses a fear: the Gentiles will mock their writing. God made them mighty in speech by the Holy Ghost, but not in writing.
They write only a little because of clumsy hands, unlike the brother of Jared, whose writings were overpowering to read.

f.g: Engraving on metal plates was slow and difficult.

chapters.n: Their spoken words were so powerful they cannot be captured in writing. When they write they see their weakness and stumble over word placement, and Moroni fears mockery.

f.w: stumble because of the placing of our words

chapters.n: The Lord replies: fools mock, but they will mourn; his grace is sufficient for the meek, so the meek will not take advantage of Moroni’s weakness.
A key promise: God gives people weakness so they will be humble. His grace is enough for all who humble themselves and have faith; then he will make weak things strong.

f.w: I give unto men weakness that they may be humble

chapters.n: God will show the Gentiles their weakness and teach them that faith, hope, and charity lead to him, the fountain of all righteousness.
Comforted, Moroni submits to God’s will, knowing God works with people according to their faith.
The brother of Jared told the mountain Zerin to move, and it moved. Without faith it would not have. God works after people have faith.
After the disciples had faith and spoke in Christ’s name, he showed himself to them in great power.
Christ has prepared a house among the Father’s mansions, giving a more excellent hope. Without hope one cannot receive that inheritance.
Christ loved the world enough to lay down his life and take it again, to prepare a place for God’s children.
This love is charity. Without charity, people cannot inherit the place Christ has prepared.
So if the Gentiles lack charity because of Moroni’s weak writing, God will test them, take away their talent, and give it to those who have more.

f.g: From the parable of the talents.

chapters.n: Moroni prays that the Gentiles will receive grace so they may have charity — praying for the very readers he fears will mock him.

The Lord says that if they lack charity, it’s not Moroni’s concern — he has been faithful, his garments will be clean, and because he saw his weakness he will be made strong and sit in the Father’s mansions.

f.w: thy garments shall be made clean

chapters.n: Moroni bids farewell to the Gentiles and to his beloved brethren until they meet at Christ’s judgment seat, where all will know he is free of their blood.

f.w: my garments are not spotted with your blood

chapters.n: Then all will know he has seen Jesus, who talked with him face to face in plain, humble language, as one man talks to another.
He has written only a few things because of his weakness in writing.
Moroni urges everyone to seek the Jesus of whom prophets and apostles wrote, so the grace of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost may abide in them forever.
Moroni resumes to finish the story of the Jaredites’ destruction.
The people rejected Ether, who taught them everything from the beginning: after the Flood’s waters receded, this land became choice above all, and all who live on it must serve the Lord.

f.w: a chosen land of the Lord

chapters.n: Ether taught that this land would be the place of the New Jerusalem that comes down from heaven, and the Lord’s holy sanctuary.

f.w: the New Jerusalem, which should come down out of heaven

chapters.n: Ether saw the days of Christ in vision and spoke of a New Jerusalem on this land — centuries before Lehi arrived.

f.w: Ether saw the days of Christ

chapters.n: He also foresaw old Jerusalem, from which Lehi would come: after its destruction it would be rebuilt as a holy city for Israel. It is not “new” because it existed long before.

f.w: the Jerusalem from whence Lehi should come

chapters.n: A New Jerusalem will be built on this land for the remnant of Joseph’s descendants — something foreshadowed by a “type.”

f.w: the remnant of the seed of Joseph

chapters.n: The type: as Joseph brought his father Jacob to Egypt and saved him from famine, God brought a remnant of Joseph’s seed (Lehi’s family) from Jerusalem so they would not perish. Mercy to the father mirrors mercy to the descendants.

f.w: Joseph brought his father down into the land of Egypt

chapters.n: Joseph’s remnant will be established in this land as their inheritance and build a holy city like Jerusalem of old; they will no longer be confounded until the earth passes away.

f.w: build up a holy city unto the Lord

chapters.n: There will be a new heaven and a new earth, like the old but made new.

f.w: a new heaven and a new earth

chapters.n: Then comes the New Jerusalem. Blessed are its inhabitants, whose garments are white through the Lamb’s blood — counted among Joseph’s remnant of Israel.

f.w: garments are white through the blood of the Lamb

chapters.n: Jerusalem of old also returns, its blessed inhabitants washed in the Lamb’s blood, gathered from the four corners of the earth and the north countries, sharing in God’s covenant with Abraham.

f.w: the covenant which God made with their father, Abraham

chapters.n: This fulfills the scripture that the first shall be last and the last first. The Gentiles, last to receive the gospel, are now first; Israel, first to receive it, will be last.

f.w: they who were first, who shall be last

chapters.n: Moroni is forbidden to write more of Ether’s great prophecies. The people treated Ether as nothing and cast him out; he hid in a cave by day and went out by night to watch what was happening.
Living in the cave, Ether wrote the rest of this record, observing the destruction by night. He is an eyewitness historian like Mormon.

f.w: made the remainder of this record

chapters.n: The same year he is cast out, a great war begins. Many powerful men use secret plans to try to destroy King Coriantumr.
Coriantumr, trained in warfare and worldly cunning, fights those who seek his life.
But he does not repent, nor do his children or the children of Cohor and Corihor — no one in the land repents. The phrase “fair sons and daughters” recalls Mormon’s lament over his people.
In Ether’s first year in the cave, many are killed by the secret combinations fighting Coriantumr for the kingdom.
Coriantumr’s sons fight hard and suffer greatly.
In the second year the Lord sends Ether to tell Coriantumr: if he and his household repent, the Lord will give him his kingdom and spare the people. Even now, God offers rescue.
Otherwise all will be destroyed except Coriantumr himself, who will live to see another people inherit the land and be buried by them.
Coriantumr, his household, and the people refuse to repent; the wars continue. They try to kill Ether, who flees back to his cave.
Shared rises up, defeats Coriantumr, and in the third year takes him captive.

f.g: A rival claimant to the throne.

chapters.n: In the fourth year Coriantumr’s sons defeat Shared and restore the kingdom to their father.
War spreads across the whole land — every man and his band fighting for what he wants. Society has collapsed into factions.
Robbers and every kind of wickedness fill the land.
Furious with Shared, Coriantumr leads his armies against him; they meet in great anger in the valley of Gilgal, and the battle is fierce.

f.g: A Jaredite valley; not the Gilgal of Joshua.

chapters.n: Shared fights for three days; Coriantumr defeats him and chases him to the plains of Heshlon.
On the plains Shared strikes back, defeating Coriantumr and driving him back to Gilgal.
In Gilgal Coriantumr fights again, defeats Shared, and kills him.
Shared wounds Coriantumr in the thigh, keeping him out of battle for two years, while everyone in the land sheds blood with no one to restrain them.
A great curse falls on the land because of wickedness: if someone sets down a tool or sword, by morning it is gone. Nothing is secure.

f.w: a great curse upon all the land

chapters.n: So everyone clings to his own belongings, refusing to borrow or lend, keeping his sword hilt in his right hand to defend property, life, and family. Trust has completely broken down.
Two years after Shared’s death, his brother attacks Coriantumr but is defeated and chased to the wilderness of Akish.

f.g: A region named after the earlier conspirator Akish (Ether 8).

chapters.n: Shared’s brother fights back in the wilderness of Akish; the battle is fierce and thousands die.
Coriantumr besieges the wilderness, but Shared’s brother slips out at night and kills part of Coriantumr’s army while they are drunk.

f.g: Surround to cut off supplies and escape.

chapters.n: He then goes to Moron and seizes Coriantumr’s throne.
Coriantumr stays in the wilderness two years, building up his army.
Shared’s brother, named Gilead, also strengthens his army through secret combinations.
Gilead’s own high priest murders him on his throne. Those who rise by secret plots fall by them.
A member of a secret combination kills the high priest in a secret pass and takes the kingdom. His name is Lib — not the earlier good king — and he is taller than anyone else.

f.g: A different man from righteous King Lib in Ether 10.
Very tall, a giant of a man.

chapters.n: In Lib’s first year, Coriantumr marches to Moron and attacks him.
Lib wounds Coriantumr’s arm, but Coriantumr’s army presses on, and Lib flees to the seashore borders.
Coriantumr pursues, and Lib fights him on the seashore.
Lib defeats Coriantumr’s army, which flees again to the wilderness of Akish.
Lib chases him to the plains of Agosh. Coriantumr takes all the people from that region with him as he flees.
At Agosh Coriantumr fights and kills Lib, but Lib’s brother takes over and drives Coriantumr back again.
Lib’s brother is Shiz. He pursues Coriantumr, overthrowing and burning cities and killing women and children.
Terror of Shiz spreads everywhere: “Who can stand before the army of Shiz? He sweeps the earth before him!”

f.g: Destroys everything in his path, like a broom.

chapters.n: People throughout the land begin to gather into armies.
The population divides, some joining Shiz and some joining Coriantumr. There is no neutral ground left.
The war has lasted so long that the land is covered with dead bodies.
The fighting is so constant that no one buries the dead; armies move from one slaughter to the next, leaving men, women, and children to decay.

f.w: a prey to the worms of the flesh

chapters.n: The stench fills the whole land, troubling people day and night. Moroni does not soften the horror of war.
Shiz keeps pursuing Coriantumr, sworn to avenge his brother — and also, unknowingly, to disprove Ether’s prophecy that Coriantumr would not die by the sword.

f.w: Coriantumr should not fall by the sword

chapters.n: Moroni comments that the Lord visited them in the fulness of his wrath; their own wickedness prepared the way for their everlasting destruction.
Shiz chases Coriantumr east to the seashore, where Coriantumr fights him for three days.
Shiz’s armies suffer such terrible losses that his people flee to the land of Corihor, sweeping away all inhabitants who won’t join them.
Shiz’s side camps in the valley of Corihor; Coriantumr camps in the valley of Shurr near the hill Comnor. He gathers his armies on the hill and sounds a trumpet to challenge Shiz.

f.g: A battle signal and formal challenge.

chapters.n: Shiz’s armies attack twice and are driven back twice; the third assault becomes a fierce battle.
Shiz gives Coriantumr many deep wounds; Coriantumr faints from blood loss and is carried off as if dead.
The losses of men, women, and children are so great on both sides that Shiz orders his people not to pursue Coriantumr’s armies, and they return to camp.
After recovering from his wounds, Coriantumr begins to remember Ether’s warnings. Memory returns, but very late.

f.w: the words which Ether had spoken

chapters.n: He realizes nearly two million of his mighty men, plus their wives and children, have died by the sword, and sorrow fills his heart.

f.g: A staggering toll — and not counting women and children.

chapters.n: He starts to repent and sees that every word of the prophets has come true so far. His soul mourns and cannot be comforted.
He writes to Shiz offering to give up the kingdom if Shiz will spare the people.
Shiz replies that he will spare the people only if Coriantumr surrenders so Shiz can kill him with his own sword. Revenge outweighs peace.
The people do not repent. Each side is stirred to anger against the other, and Shiz’s people attack.
Facing defeat, Coriantumr flees again from Shiz’s people.
He reaches the waters of Ripliancum — meaning “large” or “to exceed all” — and camps there; Shiz camps nearby, and they fight the next day.

f.g: A Jaredite name for a large body of water; the text translates it as “large, or to exceed all.”

chapters.n: In a fierce battle Coriantumr is wounded again and faints from loss of blood.
Coriantumr’s armies push back Shiz’s armies, who flee south and camp at a place called Ogath.
Coriantumr’s army camps by the hill Ramah — the same hill where Mormon later hid the sacred records. Two great nations met their end at the same hill.
Everyone left alive in the land is gathered, except Ether.
Ether watches as Coriantumr’s supporters gather to his army and Shiz’s supporters to his.
For four years they gather every person in the land to gain every possible bit of strength. Both sides prepare for total war.

f.g: Compare the Nephites gathering to Cumorah.

chapters.n: Fully gathered, men, women, and children are all armed with shields, breastplates, and helmets. They fight all day without either side winning.
At night, exhausted, they return to camp and howl and lament for their dead, so loudly the air seems torn.

f.g: Tear the air — fill it with piercing cries.

chapters.n: The next day is great and terrible; still no victory, and that night again they fill the air with cries and mourning.
Coriantumr writes to Shiz again, offering him the kingdom if he will stop fighting and spare the people.
But the Spirit of the Lord has stopped striving with them, and Satan has full power over their hearts. Given up to hard hearts and blind minds, they fight again.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord had ceased striving with them
Satan had full power over the hearts

chapters.n: They fight all day and at night sleep on their swords.

f.g: Kept weapons ready even in sleep.

chapters.n: The next day they fight until nightfall.
At night they are “drunken with anger” like men drunk on wine, and again sleep on their swords. Rage itself has become intoxicating.
The next day they fight again; by night only 52 of Coriantumr’s people and 69 of Shiz’s remain.
They sleep on their swords, and the following day fight with sword and shield all day.
By nightfall, 32 of Shiz’s people and 27 of Coriantumr’s remain.
They eat, sleep, and prepare for death the next day. They are large, powerful men — yet strength cannot save them.
They fight for three hours and faint from loss of blood.
When Coriantumr’s men regain enough strength to walk, they try to flee, but Shiz and his men rise, and Shiz swears to kill Coriantumr or die.
Shiz overtakes them the next day; they fight until only Coriantumr and Shiz remain, and Shiz faints from blood loss.
Coriantumr leans on his sword to rest a moment, then strikes off Shiz’s head.
Shiz raises himself on his hands, falls, struggles for breath, and dies. The grim detail underscores the horror of the end.

f.g: Probably an involuntary reflex at death.

chapters.n: Coriantumr collapses as though lifeless — the last Jaredite standing, exactly as Ether had prophesied.

The Lord tells Ether to go forth. He sees that all God’s words were fulfilled, finishes his record, and hides it where Limhi’s people later find it. Moroni notes he has not written even a hundredth part.

f.w: the people of Limhi did find them

chapters.n: Ether’s last words: whether the Lord translates him or he suffers God’s will in the flesh doesn’t matter, if only he is saved in God’s kingdom. A serene ending to a terrible story.

f.g: Changed so as not to taste death, like the Three Nephites.
